"Five companies in four years," Gautam said, running a finger down the CV. "Tell me what you built at each."
"Well," Sahil said. "At the first I left before the project shipped. The second offered more money. The third had a fancier name."
"And the fourth?"
"More money again. Then this one too, if I'm honest. Every move was for the salary."
Gautam put the page down. "I don't see a direction here. Lots of names, but I can't tell what you're good at. What do you want to be known for?"
Sahil opened his mouth and nothing came. His cheeks went warm.
"Take a moment," Gautam said.
The interview ended politely. A week later the email said, "We have chosen to go with another candidate."

qa.a: Sahil listed five companies in four years.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when nothing came in answer to what he wanted to be known for?
qa.a: Sahil was embarrassed and caught out, with warm cheeks, realising he had no direction to name.

qa.q: What could Sahil do differently when choosing the next move?
qa.a: Sahil could pick roles by what he will learn and build, and stay long enough to finish something.

qa.q: How might Gautam have seen Sahil's CV?
qa.a: Gautam saw many names but no clear thread, so could not tell what Sahil was good at.

grounding: The dialogue shows a person who hops to whichever company pays most, ignoring learning and reputation, and after four years has a CV with many names but little depth or direction.

I'm Zubin, and my résumé has six company names in four years. I used to be proud of that. Each move was a jump in pay: fifteen, twenty, once thirty percent. I never asked what I would learn there, or whether I'd stay long enough to finish anything.
Last month I interviewed for a senior role. The panel asked, 'Tell us about a system you built and looked after over time.' I didn't have one. I had pieces of six systems, none of them mine. Then, 'What's your area?' I said, 'A bit of everything.' I saw the look.
My friend Vishal, who stayed at one company and switched teams inside it, has just become a tech lead. He earns a little less than me. He has a direction. I have a pay slip.

qa.q: How many company names are on Zubin's résumé?
qa.a: Six company names in four years.

qa.q: What did Zubin feel when saying 'A bit of everything' and seeing the look?
qa.a: Zubin felt embarrassed and exposed, realising the frequent moves had left no depth or clear area.

qa.q: What would you advise Zubin to weigh before the next move?
qa.a: What a role would teach and whether it builds depth in one area, not just the size of the pay rise.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Zubin's path?
qa.a: Vishal may feel sympathy, having chosen growth inside one company, and may see that higher pay hasn't given Zubin direction.

grounding: It shows someone who hopped to the highest-paying company each time, ending up with many employers but little depth or direction.

Mentor's note after a career session, 12 February.
Manoj came in asking how to get a lead role. His CV shows five employers in four years, each move for a higher salary. I asked him to describe one project from start to finish. He described the start of three and the finish of none. When I asked what he wanted to be known for, he said, 'Being well paid,' then laughed, then went quiet.
He admitted two recent interviews ended with the same feedback: good range, no depth. I asked him to list what he had actually enjoyed in each job. The same word came up three times: data. We agreed he would look at roles by what they would teach him in data over two years, not only by pay, and talk to me again in a month.
Ojas

qa.q: How many employers does Manoj's CV show?
What does Manoj laughing and then going quiet suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, noticing that pay alone was a thin answer.

qa.q: What approach did Manoj and Ojas agree on instead?
qa.a: Choosing roles by what they would teach him in data over two years, not only by pay.

qa.q: How might the interviewers have seen Manoj's CV?
qa.a: They saw good range but no depth, so they doubted he could own a system or lead a team.

grounding: It shows a mentor's note on someone who kept moving for the highest pay and now has many employers but little depth or direction.
